en: The Shorter Exposition;
The Exposition of the Chapter on the Way to the Far Shore;
The Exposition of the Questions.
10. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Brahmin Kappa "Standing in the midst of the lake," [said the Venerable Kappa].
When a flood has arisen, full of great terror,
for those overcome by old age and death,
tell me, O Venerable One, what is the island?
And you, explain to me this island, so that there may be no further becoming.

"Standing in the midst of the lake": here "lake" refers to *saṃsāra*—coming and going, coming and going back, time, destiny, existence and non-existence, death and rebirth, arising and dissolution, birth, aging, and death.
Neither the prior limit nor the subsequent limit of saṃsāra is discerned;
beings in the midst of saṃsāra alone are stationed, established, attached, arrived at, clinging, and intent upon it.
How is it that the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned?
"It is not the case that the round has turned for this many births and will not turn beyond that; thus too, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.
It is not the case that the round has turned for this many hundreds of births and will not turn beyond that; thus too, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.
It is not the case that the round has turned for this many thousands of births and will not turn beyond that; thus too, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned."
"It is not the case that the round has turned for this many hundreds of thousands of births and will not turn beyond that; thus, even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
It is not the case that the round has turned for this many millions of births and will not turn beyond that; thus, even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
It is not the case that the round has turned for this many hundreds of millions of births and will not turn beyond that; thus, even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known."
"It is not the case that the round has turned for this many thousands of millions of births and will not turn beyond that;
thus, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.
It is not the case that the round has turned for this many hundreds of thousands of millions of births and will not turn beyond that; thus, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned."
There is no such thing as saying, "The cycle of existence has turned for this many years and will not turn beyond that," for even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
There is no such thing as saying, "The cycle of existence has turned for this many hundreds of years and will not turn beyond that," for even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
There is no such thing as saying, "The cycle of existence has turned for this many thousands of years and will not turn beyond that," for even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
"It is not the case that the round has turned for this many hundreds of thousands of years and will not turn beyond that; thus, even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.
It is not the case that the round has turned for this many millions of years and will not turn beyond that; thus, even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.
It is not the case that the round has turned for this many hundreds of millions of years and will not turn beyond that; thus, even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned."
"There were this many thousands of millions of years during which the cycle turned, and after that it did not turn"—there is no such thing; thus, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
"There were this many hundreds of thousands of millions of years during which the cycle turned, and after that it did not turn"—there is no such thing; thus, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
"There were this many eons during which the cycle turned, and after that it did not turn"—there is no such thing; thus, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
"It is not the case that the cycle has turned for this many hundreds of eons and will not turn beyond that; thus, even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
It is not the case that the cycle has turned for this many thousands of eons and will not turn beyond that; thus, even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known.
It is not the case that the cycle has turned for this many hundreds of thousands of eons and will not turn beyond that; thus, even in this way, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not known."
"There have been this many millions of aeons during which the cycle turned, and beyond that it did not turn"—there is no such thing; thus, too, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.

"There have been this many hundreds of millions of aeons during which the cycle turned, and beyond that it did not turn"—there is no such thing; thus, too, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.

"There have been this many thousands of millions of aeons during which the cycle turned, and beyond that it did not turn"—there is no such thing; thus, too, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.
For so many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons the cycle has turned; that it will not turn beyond this is not the case. Thus, too, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning; a first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.”
"Thus, monks, for a long time suffering has been experienced, intense suffering has been experienced, calamity has been experienced, and the charnel ground has increased.
To this extent, monks, it is indeed enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, and enough to be liberated from them.
In this way, too, the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.
How is it that the furthest limit of saṃsāra is not known?

It is because there is no such thing as saying, "The round of existence will continue for this many births, and beyond that it will not continue. In this way, too, the furthest limit of saṃsāra is not known.
[It is not known] whether there are this many hundreds of births, this many thousands of births, this many hundreds of thousands of births... [and so on].
so many millions of births, so many hundreds of millions of births, so many thousands of millions of births,
so many hundreds of thousands of millions of births; so many years, so many hundreds of years, so many thousands of years, so many hundreds of thousands of years,
so many tens of millions of years, so many hundreds of tens of millions of years, so many...
For thousands of millions of years, for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, for so many eons, for so many hundreds of eons,
for so many thousands of eons, for so many hundreds of thousands of eons, for so many millions of eons, for so many hundreds of millions of eons,
for so many thousands of millions of eons, and for so many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, the cycle of existence [continues].
"It will continue, and beyond that it will not continue"—there is no such thing. Thus, even in this way, the furthest limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.

Likewise, even the prior limit of saṃsāra is not discerned, nor is its furthest limit discerned; rather, beings in the midst of saṃsāra alone stand, are established, cling, have approached, are attached to, and are intent upon it—standing in the middle of the stream.
"Thus the Venerable Kappa.
"Thus" (*iccā*) is a grammatical conjunction (*padasandhi*)... [etc.
"Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment... [etc.]
"Kappa" is the name, ...pe... the designation of that brahmin—thus said the Venerable Kappa.

"When the flood has arisen, the great terror": when the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance have arisen, come into being, been produced, been generated, and become manifest.
"Great terrors" refers to the fear of birth, the fear of aging, the fear of illness,
and the fear of death— when the flood has arisen,
these are the great terrors. "Of those overcome by aging and death" means of those who are touched by aging, who are beset, confounded, and possessed [by them].
"Of those touched by death, overcome, bewildered, and possessed; followed by birth, pursued by aging, overwhelmed by sickness, and struck down by death;
without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and having become without refuge"—this refers to "those overcome by aging and death."

"Tell me, dear sir, of an island"—that is, tell, declare, show, point out, establish, reveal, analyze, make clear, explain, and manifest an island, a refuge, a shelter, a resort, a destination, and a final support.
"Dear sir" (*mārisa*) is a term of endearment, a term of respect; it is a designation for one who is revered and held in high esteem. Thus:
"Tell me, dear sir, of an island."
"And you, tell me of an island.
He says "you" to the Blessed One. "Tell me of an island" means:
tell, declare, show, point out, establish, set forth, reveal, analyze, make plain, and explain an island—a refuge, a shelter, a resort, a destination, and a final support.
And you, explain the light to me:

how this [suffering] might not come to be again; that is, how this suffering might cease right here, be stilled, go to its end, be subsided, and how suffering involving rebirth-linking would no longer be produced within the realm of sense-desire (*kāmadhātu*).
or in the form realm, or in the formless realm; or in the existence of sensual desire, or in the existence of form, or in the existence of the formless;

or in the existence of perception, or in the existence of non-perception, or in the existence of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; or in the existence of one constituent, or in the existence of four constituents, or in the existence of five constituents;
or in a future destination, or in rebirth, or in reconnection, or in becoming, or in saṃsāra, or in the cycle—[he] would not generate [craving].
It would not be produced, it would not come into being, it would not be generated.
It would cease right here, be stilled, go to its end, and be subsided—
so that there would be no further state of existence.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“Standing in the middle of the lake,” (thus said the Venerable Kappa).
When a flood has arisen, full of great terror,
for those overcome by old age and death,
tell us, O Venerable One, of an island.
"And you, tell me the island,
so that there may be no further becoming for me," as he stood in the midst of the lake.
(The Blessed One said:
"When the flood has arisen, in the great terror,
for those overcome by old age and death,"
"I call you an island for an eon.

"Standing in the midst of a lake"—here, "lake" refers to *saṃsāra*: coming and going, going and coming, time, destiny, existence and non-existence, falling away and rebirth, arising and dissolution, birth, aging, and death.
Neither the prior limit nor the subsequent limit of *saṃsāra* is discerned.
Beings are situated, established, attached, involved, clinging, and intent upon the midst of *saṃsāra*.
How is it that the prior limit of *saṃsāra* is not discerned?
… [as before] … thus the prior limit of *saṃsāra* is not discerned.
How is it that the furthest limit of saṃsāra is not discerned? ...
[as before] ... Thus the furthest limit of saṃsāra is not discerned.
In this way, neither the prior limit nor the furthest limit of saṃsāra is discerned.
"Beings who stand, are established, cling, have approached, are attached to, and are intent upon the midst of saṃsāra—
these are 'those standing in the middle of the stream.
'Eons,' O Blessed One."
"Kappa," said the Blessed One, addressing that brahmin by name.
"Bhagavā" is a term of respect... [as above] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely "Bhagavā"—thus said the Blessed One.

"When the floods have arisen, the great terrors": when the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance have arisen, been produced, come into being, been fully manifested, and become apparent.
"The great terrors" refers to the fear of birth, the fear of aging, the fear of illness, and the fear of death—thus, "when the floods have arisen, the great terrors."
"Of those overcome by old age and death" means: of those touched by old age, overtaken, confounded, and possessed;
of those touched by death, overtaken, confounded, and possessed; of those followed by birth, pursued by old age, overcome by sickness, and struck down by death;
who are without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and have become without refuge.
"For those overcome by old age and death, I declare an island;

I call it an island, O Kappa. I call it a refuge, a shelter, a resort, a destination, and a final resort; I proclaim, I point out, I teach, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I make plain, and I manifest it—thus, 'I declare an island;
I call it an island, O Kappa.'"
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For those standing in the middle of a lake,” [the Blessed One said,] “...for aeons.”
When a flood has arisen, full of great terror,
for those overcome by old age and death,
I declare you to be an island for an eon.
Possessing nothing, grasping at nothing—
this is the island, beyond which there is none other;
I call it Nibbāna.
The complete destruction of old age and death.
"Nothing and no grasping"— here,
"something" (kiñcana) means:
The trinket of lust, the trinket of hatred, the trinket of delusion, the trinket of conceit, the trinket of views, the trinket of defilements, and the trinket of misconduct;

the abandoning of these trinkets, the pacification of these trinkets, the relinquishing of these trinkets, and the subsiding of these trinkets— the deathless Nibbāna— is "possessing nothing" (akiñcana).
"Non-clinging": "Clinging" is said to be craving—that which is lust, infatuation, covetousness, greed, and the root of unwholesomeness.
The abandoning of clinging, the stilling of clinging, the relinquishing of clinging, the subsiding of clinging, is the deathless Nibbāna.
Possessing nothing, grasping at nothing—this is the island, the one without another;
this is the island, the refuge, the shelter, the resort, the destination, the ultimate goal.
"Without another" means there is no other island beyond it.
Then, regarding this island as foremost, best, most excellent, preeminent, supreme, and sublime—one says:
"This is the island; there is no other beyond it;
we call it Nibbāna. Here, "vāna" is said to mean craving.
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... pe ... covetousness, greed, and root of unwholesomeness there is—that is [the "desire"].
The abandoning of desire, the stilling of desire, the relinquishing of desire, the subsiding of desire, the deathless Nibbāna—that is [the "non-desire"].
"Iti" (thus) is the connection of words, the conjunction of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of phonemes, and the sequential order of words.
"Thus," he says: "I say, I declare, I proclaim, I teach, I make known, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I make plain, I elucidate"—thus do I say: "It is Nibbāna."

"The complete destruction of aging and death" means: the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, the calming, the deathless Nibbāna of aging and death—this is "the complete destruction of aging and death.
Thus the Blessed One said.
“Possessing nothing, grasping at nothing—
this is an island with no beyond;
I call it Nibbāna.”
"the exhaustion of old age and death"—
having understood this, those who are mindful are extinguished even in this very life.
They do not follow Mara’s sway;
they are not followers in Mara’s path—
those who know this are the mindful ones.
So much is this Deathless Nibbāna:
that which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
"Having known" means having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully realized it, [thinking]: "All formations are impermanent," and so forth...

“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation”—having known this, having understood it, having weighed it, having scrutinized it, having made it manifest, and having brought it to full clarity.
Thus, the Arahants are those whose taints are exhausted.
They are mindful by way of four causes:
Those who, developing the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body,
are mindful … [and so on] … they are called "the mindful"—
those who are mindful having understood this.
"Extinguished in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā*):
"In this very life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) means the Dhamma has been seen, known, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and fully manifested.
"Extinguished" (*abhinibbutā*) means extinguished because of the extinction of lust, [extinguished] because of the extinction of hatred... [and so on].

Because all unwholesome volitional formations have been calmed, stilled, tranquillized, extinguished, quenched, and subsided; because they are calm, stilled, tranquillized, quenched, and subsided—one is “quenched in this very life” (diṭṭhadhammābhinibbuta).
Such a one does not follow the power of Māra.
"Māra" refers to that Māra who is Kaṇha, the Overlord, the End-maker, Namuci, the Kinsman of the Negligent.
They are not subject to Māra’s power; they do not live under Māra’s control, nor does Māra exercise control over them.
They have overcome Māra, the faction of Māra, the snare of Māra, the trap of Māra, the bait of Māra, the domain of Māra, and the dwelling-place of Māra.
Having overcome, having conquered, having overwhelmed, having exhausted, and having crushed both the domain of Māra and the bondage of Māra,
they move, dwell, conduct themselves, proceed, protect, maintain, sustain, and carry on; thus,
they are not followers under the sway of Māra.
"You are not followers of Māra"— meaning you will not be those who follow in Māra's footsteps or his attendants;
"you will be followers of the Blessed Buddha"— meaning you will be those who follow in the Buddha's footsteps or his attendants—
thus, "you are not followers of Māra."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Having understood this, those who are mindful are extinguished in the present life."
“They do not follow Mara’s sway;
they are not followers in Mara’s path.
At the conclusion of this verse... [pe]...
"The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.
This concludes the tenth exposition: The Questions of Kappa the Young Man.
